item.title: Unions in Italy for Nordic employers: less negotiation, more agreement
item.description: Nordic companies are used to local union cooperation. In Italy, unions act mainly through national agreements. What a small foreign employer actually meets.

item.title: Flat hierarchy meets Italian workplace culture: feedback and decisions
item.description: Nordic managers lead by consensus and understatement. Italian colleagues often expect clearer direction and warmer contact. Practical habits for mixed teams.

item.title: July at home, August in Italy: planning holiday coverage across both calendars
item.description: Nordic offices empty in July, Italian ones in August. How to use the offset, plan public holidays and keep customers covered all summer.

item.title: Reading an Italian payslip (busta paga) as a Nordic manager
item.description: The Italian payslip has more lines than a Swedish lönespecifikation. What each block means, so you can answer your employee and check the invoice.

item.title: Sick leave in Italy for Nordic managers: no karensavdrag, a different certificate
item.description: In Sweden the employer pays 80% sick pay for 14 days after a qualifying deduction. In Italy the doctor certifies online to INPS. What a manager may ask.

item.title: Parental leave: from 480 Swedish days to the Italian model
item.description: Nordic parental leave is long and shared. Italy has a compulsory maternity period, a short paternity leave and optional leave on top. How to plan the team.
